item.title: Australia’s Version of Halloween: Spring, Sunshine and Skepticism
item.description:
The days are getting longer, spring is coming into bloom — and hordes of trick-or-treaters are making their rounds well before dark. This is Halloween in Australia, and it can look a lot different from the American version.

Though some Australians still feel that Halloween is an unwelcome American import, it has become increasingly popular, particularly for children (and their occasionally begrudging parents.)

To Geri Wee, who lives in the eastern suburbs of Melbourne, a good barometer of the holiday’s growing appeal is the sheer volume of candy her two children receive — so much that they’re still working through their stash from two years ago.

“It’s good for the kids,” Ms. Wee said. “And it’s great for the dentist.”

In a hemisphere where October heralds the approach of summer, there are no fall colors and temperatures are mostly warm. Australian children typically go trick-or-treating right after school, in broad daylight.

“It’s not a spooky thing. You can’t hide anywhere because it’s so light,” said Simon Thomas, a recovery specialist at a life insurance company who lives in Parkdale, a suburb in Melbourne’s southeast. “Sometimes we’ve been caught out where the kids are boiling because it’s too hot in their costumes.”

Jack-o’-lanterns are also less common, though they’re coming into fashion. Many Australian pumpkin varieties are dense, hard-skinned and harvested earlier in the year, so supermarket chains have taken to importing decorative pumpkins that are better suited for carving, or sourcing them from local growers.

And while the holiday is being embraced at an official level — local councils organize events and designate areas where costumed children are welcome — trick-or-treaters cannot assume a welcome at every door.

“The practice of trick-or-treating is uneven across suburbs, with decorations on houses signaling that it’s OK to come ask for treats,” said Rodney Taveira, a senior lecturer in American studies at the University of Sydney. “There might be whole streets that are unadorned.”

That patchy embrace reflects a longstanding debate over whether Australia should adopt a tradition that critics regard as American cultural encroachment — a debate rigorous enough to merit serious market research.

Polling from YouGov published this week showed just over half of the 1,000 Australians surveyed intended to celebrate Halloween, even as 69 percent called it an “unnecessary import from the United States” and 63 percent said they would rather not have trick-or-treaters come to their door.

Mr. Taveira traced Halloween’s growing popularity in Australia to the 2000s, when American movies like “Mean Girls,” which features a Halloween party, became cultural touchstones. A combination of social media and advertising campaigns by retailers have since helped promote the holiday, he said, and resistance to it has eased over the past decade.

Kelsey Smith, who lives in Sydney, said she has seen Australia embrace Halloween since she relocated from Oregon 16 years ago.

“When I moved here, there was no one who did Halloween,” said Ms. Smith, whose home is in the northern suburb of Manly. Now, she said, Australians go one of two ways: “Either people are all in or totally out.”

But Halloween is unlikely to reach the commercial scale it has in the United States, where it is part of a shopping season that leads into Thanksgiving and the year-end holidays, said Lauren Rosewarne, an associate professor at the University of Melbourne who studies media and pop culture.

In Australia it remains a largely stand-alone event, she said, with retailers focusing mainly on candy, known locally as lollies — though the hardware chain Bunnings, a national staple, now stocks an extensive range of Halloween products.

Americans were expected to spend over $13.5 billion on Halloween this year, according to the National Retail Federation. Candy, decorations and costumes are the main spending categories.

To Ms. Rosewarne, it was unclear why Halloween had become a flashpoint over American influence, given how much other American culture Australia embraces — and the fact that the holiday is celebrated beyond the United States.

“It feels rather arbitrary that this is the one thing we don’t want from America,” she said.

The conversation has quieted in recent years, Ms. Rosewarne said, as Australians have confronted more pressing concerns about their country’s relationship with the United States under President Trump.

And for parents with children, it can be hard to resist the holiday’s charms.

“It’s part of the calendar that people look forward to now, just like Christmas,” said Ms. Wee, adding that in recent years she had noticed more houses decorated for Halloween in her area.

Mr. Thomas and his wife, Kim — whose three children planned to dress up as characters from the Quentin Tarantino film “Kill Bill” on Saturday — said the debate about whether to embrace Halloween had tailed off over the years.

When Halloween was first becoming popular, there was backlash along the lines of “‘it’s very American, we don’t do this,’” Mr. Thomas said. “But the people that probably say that then have kids and start to think that’s it’s actually quite cute and fun.”

Matthew Abbott contributed reporting.

item.title: Global Talks on Nature End With Persistent Gaps on Action and Funding
item.description:
Two weeks of global negotiations to protect the world’s wildlife and ecosystems ended on Saturday in Yerevan, Armenia, with nations reaffirming their pledges to protect nature but still off track to meet an ambitious set of targets by a 2030 deadline.

Biodiversity, the variety of life on the planet, is declining at levels unprecedented in human history, scientists say.

In 2022, in a landmark agreement made under the United Nations biodiversity treaty, nations pledged to reverse those losses by taking action on 23 targets, including protecting 30 percent of the earth’s land and water and reforming industries that drive declines in wildlife.

This year’s meeting marked the halfway point for countries to meet their deadline for those pledges. The United States is the only country, with the exception of the Vatican, that is not party to the treaty, though it attends the meeting and participates from the sidelines.

Just before the talks began, the United Nations issued a review of progress that found that countries were lagging far behind. A major theme was how to get on track with a “Yerevan Pathway” that would help unlock progress.

In the end, delegates reaffirmed their commitments and set priorities, creating pressure for domestic action, but tense questions over how to pay for nature protection, especially in countries that are poor financially but rich in biodiversity, remained unresolved.

Countries pledged almost $2 billion in new financing, conference officials said.

“Within the inevitable limits of the U.N. system, I think that we’ve made some significant progress,” said Steven Guilbeault, a former environment minister of Canada who helped shepherd through the 2022 global biodiversity agreement. He was heartened to see more finance ministers in Yerevan, he said, because action on biodiversity requires their involvement.

A major highlight, he and others said, was a focus on tackling one of the thorniest issues: about $2.4 trillion in public money that flows toward environmentally damaging activities, according to the United Nations.

“Armenia deserves credit for touching the ‘third rail’ of biodiversity negotiations: the agricultural, fisheries and other subsidies that prop up a system leaving biodiversity in global decline,” said Alfred DeGemmis, the director of international policy at the nonprofit Wildlife Conservation Society.

Those harmful subsidies are seen as critical to plugging the yawning gap in funding needed for conservation, estimated at about $1.3 trillion a year by the Paulson Institute, a research organization, and others. Going into the talks, of all the pledges nations made in 2022, subsidy reform has proved one of the most difficult for countries to address.

During the talks in Yerevan, three initiatives were started to help countries make progress on reforming subsidies. One is a coalition led by Colombia and Finland that aims to bring ministerial teams together to share knowledge, experience and strategies.

“We don’t need to spend more to close the biodiversity funding gap, we need to spend better,” Marina Von Weissenberg, a Finnish senior ministerial adviser and co-chair of that effort, said in a news release. “Governments have a real opportunity here to reshape public spending with future generations in mind, but they can’t do it alone. International coordination is key to giving governments the confidence to lead change.”

Another topic of negotiations was one of the major accomplishments from the last global biodiversity talks, in Cali, Colombia, in 2024: a fund through which the pharmaceutical and other industries that rely on biodiversity would contribute to conservation efforts. Since its beginning in 2025, the effort has struggled, raising only about $10,000. Delegates in Yerevan reaffirmed the suggested rate of contribution for large companies: 1 percent of profit. But contributing to the fund is voluntary, and it remains to be seen what will happen.

Throughout the talks, some activists expressed bitter disappointment, raising concerns that the 2022 global agreement would go the way of its predecessor, which failed to fully meet a single global target.

The next such gathering will be held in 2028 in Ecuador.

item.title: Mass Protest Expected in New Delhi Over Modi and Voter Roll Changes
item.description:
Tens of thousands of demonstrators are expected to converge on India’s capital on Sunday in a display of mass resistance to the government of Prime Minister Narendra Modi and recent changes to the voter roll.

The event, organized by India’s largest opposition political party, the Indian National Congress, will be the latest in a string of large protests to ripple through New Delhi since this summer.

The demonstrators have marched under different banners, with separate leaders and demands. But they have all expressed unhappiness with Mr. Modi’s nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party, which has led India since 2014, and its initiative to update India’s voter rolls. The protesters have accused Mr. Modi of “vote theft,” claiming that his party is using its powers to try to rig the rolls in its favor.

“B.J.P., Modi — all are trying to demolish our rights, our constitution,” said Mohammed Shamin, 40, a private tutor from Delhi who planned to attend. As he mingled among the several hundred people who had started to gather at the demonstration site in central New Delhi on Saturday evening, Mr. Shamin said he was optimistic that their presence would make a difference.

“Every cloud has a silver lining,” he added, gesturing to the early arrivals and the large empty field behind them that organizers expected would be crammed by morning with people from all over India.

Organizers have said they expect as many as a million people to attend, but police officials have provided a much lower estimate of 50,000. Laborers worked through the night on Saturday to prepare the open-air venue, which was still waterlogged from heavy rain earlier in the week.

The revision of India’s voter rolls began last year in what the government has described as a routine effort to eliminate duplicates, dead people and other discrepancies. It has amounted to a sweeping overhaul, with more than 130 million names expunged so far.

Millions of people have said they were included in the purge by mistake, leading critics of Mr. Modi and the B.J.P. to accuse him of tampering with India’s electoral system and undermining the fundamental mechanism of its democracy ahead of elections in several large states next year.

Mr. Modi and his allies in the B.J.P. say their political opponents are looking for an excuse to foment unrest, which began in force in July under the banner of the Gen Z-led “cockroach” movement. The Cockroach Janta Party — named as a satirical response to a comment from India’s chief justice about “youngsters like cockroaches who don’t get any employment” — first mobilized young people across India to protest the government’s mishandling of important student entrance exams.

More recent protests have focused on the voter rolls and have largely been led not by the cockroach movement, but by the Congress party and its leader, Rahul Gandhi, the scion of India’s most illustrious political dynasty.

Sudhanshu Trivedi, national spokesman for the B.J.P., on Saturday called the Congress party’s efforts a failed attempt to “to create anarchy in India.” The B.J.P. has called its own counterprotest on Sunday and vowed to combat what it called “the falsehoods, conspiracies and unrest engineered by a desperate opposition.”

Security forces and police officers responded to the earlier protests by locking down the heart of New Delhi, detaining protest leaders and rounding up demonstrators by the thousands. The Delhi police have assigned thousands of personnel to cover the event.

Hari Kumar contributed reporting from New Delhi.

item.title: What to Know About Tensions Between Ethiopia and Eritrea
item.description:
Ethiopia and Eritrea may be marching toward a new conflict, with uncertain repercussions across the Horn of Africa and beyond.

It was only a few years ago that the countries made common cause in a war against the Tigray People’s Liberation Front. Now, fighting has erupted once again in Tigray, but this time Ethiopia and Eritrea are on opposing sides.

Ethiopia told the United Nations on Oct. 9 that Eritrea had invaded its territory in support of the Front. Eritrea denied the accusation and asked the U.N. Security Council to condemn what it described as Ethiopia’s “deplorable declaration of war.”

The countries recently severed diplomatic relations.

The hostilities have caused global alarm. Ethiopia’s population is the second largest in Africa, and each side has powerful allies. It could also expand the interlocking conflicts that stretch across the Horn of Africa and the Middle East, including wars and insurgencies in Sudan, Somalia and Yemen.

For weeks, Ethiopia and Eritrea appeared to be heading for an imminent conflict, though the immediate threat seems to have receded for the moment.

ERITREA

YEMEN

SUDAN

Mekelle

Assab

TIGRAY

REGION

DJIBOUTI

Addis Ababa

ETHIOPIA

SOMALIA

KENYA

500 miles

The New York Times

There have been decades of hostility between the two countries.

The country that is now Eritrea fought a long war for independence, which it gained in 1993. Ethiopia and Eritrea fought a border war from 1998 to 2000. A stunning reconciliation occurred in 2018, and Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed of Ethiopia was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize.

Eritrea and Ethiopia allied with each other to fight the Tigray People’s Liberation Front in 2020. Human rights groups accused Eritrea of committing some of the worst atrocities in that conflict.

More recently, Eritrea has moved closer to an alliance with Tigray, in part because it is a bulwark against Ethiopia’s stated ambition to secure access to the Red Sea. Since Eritrea won independence, Ethiopia has been landlocked and Mr. Abiy has described Red Sea access as a national imperative. The port of Assab in Eritrea is just 45 miles from Ethiopia’s border.

In mid-October, Secretary of State Marco Rubio held calls with Mr. Abiy and said that all countries in the region must “avoid cross-border incursions” and respect “the territorial integrity of their neighbors.” A similar message was delivered to Eritrea, a State Department spokesman said.

Analysts say that Mr. Rubio’s direct warning may have served to halt any move toward war, at least in the short term.

Russia’s foreign minister, Sergey V. Lavrov, has offered to mediate between the two African nations. After meeting with President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia during the Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow, Mr. Abiy said on social media that Russia had delivered 12 fighter jets to Ethiopia and would also send air defense systems.

Most of the recent fighting has been between the Ethiopian Army and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front in the north.

The Front dominated Ethiopia’s politics for decades until 2018, when Mr. Abiy came to power.

In September, the Front and six other armed opposition groups formed a coalition, the Alliance for Survival, to topple Mr. Abiy and reform the Constitution.

At first, the Alliance made gains, but federal forces turned the tables, capturing the Tigrayan capital, Mekelle, and other towns in the province and advancing to the Eritrean border.

The federal government set up a caretaker administration in Tigray, but fighting has spread to other parts of the region. On Friday, witnesses said that a drone strike in the Tigrayan town of Rama, which is not under federal control, killed 14 civilians, including a child.

Eritrea’s allies include Egypt, which has criticized Ethiopia for building a giant dam on the Nile. Other Eritrean allies include the Sudanese Armed Forces and Saudi Arabia.

President Isaias Afwerki of Eritrea traveled to Saudi Arabia for talks late last year and also met in Egypt recently with the leaders of Somalia and the Sudanese Armed Forces.

Ethiopia has accused Egypt and Sudan of backing the Tigrayan rebels, which they deny.

Ethiopia has close ties with the United Arab Emirates, a major investor in the country. In Sudan, the Emirates is widely accused of backing the Rapid Support Forces, a paramilitary group that is fighting the Sudanese military in a catastrophic civil war.

Analysts warn that a renewed conflict in Ethiopia could effectively merge with the civil war in Sudan along their shared border, with rival interests from foreign powers such as the U.A.E., Egypt and Saudi Arabia competing by proxy.

Brian O. Otieno contributed reporting from Nairobi.

item.title: Iran Braces for More War, No Matter the Outcome of the U.S. and Israeli Elections
item.description:
Little is clear about the power dynamics that will govern Israel and the United States in the coming months after pivotal elections in both countries. But Iran’s leaders are watching the contests closely, analysts said, and bracing for a renewed round of conflict whatever the outcome.

In Israel, this week’s national elections showed that neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s far-right alliance nor the main opposition bloc, led by Gadi Eisenkot, the country’s former top military official, won enough votes to form a government. That has set the stage for weeks of uncertainty.

In the United States, Democrats appear to be in a strong position to take control of at least the House in the midterm elections next week. But the exact size of their win, and whether they secure a majority in the Senate, will determine if they can put a brake on President Trump’s policies, including the war with Iran.

Tehran expects more attacks regardless of who takes control in Israel or of Congress, and has shown little willingness to make concessions demanded by the Trump administration to seal a peace deal.

On Saturday, Mojtaba Khamenei, Iran’s supreme leader, said on social media that he had met with senior leaders of the armed forces and directed them to respond to any kind or level of threat with an immediate response in order to establish “maximum deterrence.” He also directed them to be prepared to target all types of U.S. and Israeli assets.

“They have been expecting a new round of war already for a few weeks, and they’ve been preparing accordingly,” Hamidreza Azizi, senior Iran analyst at the International Crisis Group, said of the Iranian government.

In Israel, Iran would welcome the removal of Mr. Netanyahu from power, said Mohammad Saleh Sedghian, director of the Arab Center for Iranian Studies in Tehran. The Israeli leader helped persuade Mr. Trump to attack Iran this year and sought to orchestrate new airstrikes on Iran ahead of the election. But Iranian leaders believe that changing prime ministers would probably have an impact only in the short term rather than leading to a fundamental shift in Israeli policy, Mr. Sedghian said.

“Iranian and Israeli policies toward each other have remained consistent regardless of which government has been in power in Israel since the 1980s,” he said. “Any changes would likely be temporary rather than strategic.”

Mr. Azizi said that there were several scenarios for how the Israeli election results could unfold but that “we should not expect a fundamental change in the hostility between Israel and Iran.”

Even if Mr. Eisenkot or another opposition leader takes power and shifts Israel back into deploying covert tactics against Iran rather than all-out war, Iran’s response could still be escalatory.

“The Islamic Republic’s strategic thinking has undergone a significant shift, involving, first and foremost, a greater willingness to take risks and a move away from its long-established policy of strategic patience,” Mr. Azizi said. “As a result, Iran could still respond to indirect Israeli operations through direct military action.”

When it comes to the United States, Iran’s leaders are keenly aware of how the costs of the war, including higher gasoline prices for Americans, have affected Mr. Trump’s popularity and the Republican Party’s prospects in the midterms. Their assessment appears to be that a deal with Iran would benefit Mr. Trump politically, giving Tehran leverage in any negotiations to end the war. Iran, on the other hand, has already borne enormous costs including worsening inflation, without its leaders changing their stance.

Mostafa Najafi, an analyst who is said to be close to Mohsen Rezaei, the top national security adviser, wrote on social media on Wednesday that the Trump administration was pursuing a deal with Iran in the days leading up to the midterms as Republicans face a difficult fight to retain control of Congress.

“They want to leverage the agreement for the elections and insist that nuclear concessions also be part of the pre-election deal, which Tehran does not accept,” Mr. Najafi wrote. “If no agreement is reached in the next two days, the atmosphere will likely shift toward confrontation in the first week after the elections.”

Last week, Vice President JD Vance sent a letter to a top Iranian official to propose a new round of comprehensive peace talks, a senior U.S. official and an Iranian official with knowledge of the communication have said. Mr. Vance bypassed Iran’s elected government and President Masoud Pezeshkian and instead addressed the letter to Mr. Rezaei, the former longtime commander of the powerful Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps. The outreach to Mr. Rezaei reflected the Trump administration’s view that it needs to deal directly with an Iranian official with influence over hard-liners, who have opposed agreeing to a deal.

On Friday, a Qatari delegation arrived in Tehran for talks, Iran’s state news outlet reported. Qatar has been mediating discussions between Iran and the United States.

On Saturday, Abbas Araghchi, Iran’s foreign minister, said that the country’s diplomats were meeting with mediators in Doha, Qatar, Al Jazeera reported. Mr. Araghchi said Iran was reviewing proposals on its nuclear program, the report added, and he described the letter from Mr. Vance as “a positive step.”

The burst of recent diplomacy comes at a significant moment. Mr. Trump has been weighing whether to renew attacks on Iran, potentially after the midterms, and the United States and Israel have drawn up specific plans for new strikes, U.S. officials and other people briefed on the deliberations have said. But there are major obstacles that would need to be overcome for the United States and Iran to reach a final agreement.

“The two sides remain far apart on several critical issues, including the Strait of Hormuz, sanctions relief, oversight by the International Atomic Energy Agency and the scope of Iran’s nuclear commitments,” said Mehrzad Boroujerdi, an Iran expert at Missouri University of Science and Technology. “My sense is that Tehran will pursue a dual-track strategy, engaging in intermittent diplomatic negotiations while simultaneously preparing, to the best of its ability, for a possible resumption of hostilities.”

Mr. Najafi, in his social media post on Wednesday, said that Iran “insists on the fulfillment of its seven conditions” before agreeing to any interim deal. Iranian officials have referred frequently to the conditions in the past month without fully explaining what they are, and framed them as a prerequisite for new talks or the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, the critical shipping waterway on Iran’s southern coast.

Mr. Najafi said in a voice message to The New York Times that the conditions included lifting the U.S. naval blockade on Iran and sanctions on Iran’s oil sales; ending the war on all fronts, including in Lebanon, where Israel has been fighting with Hezbollah, the Iran-backed armed group; releasing frozen Iranian assets; and accepting Iran’s management of the Strait of Hormuz.

“Iran has put forth these to the American side as preconditions for the opening of the Strait of Hormuz,” Mr. Najafi said. “The American side must first fulfill these preconditions, and then the negotiations will enter the main phase.”

Mr. Najafi also expressed deep pessimism about the prospects of a lasting agreement between the two sides, saying that Iranian officials have no trust in American intentions or promises.

“Here, the messages exchanged with the United States are viewed with profound skepticism,” he said. “The issue of Iran-U.S. relations has become so complex that even if Iran were to agree to nuclear negotiations and make concessions, it is highly unlikely that this tangled web of conflict between the two nations will reach a meaningful resolution or result in a lasting agreement.”

Leily Nikounazar contributed reporting.

]]>

item.title: How Locals and Shopkeepers Tried to Save One Paris Street From Rioters
item.description:
The shattered glass, bits of metal and discarded groceries strewed across Rue Beaurepaire have been swept up. The smoke from fires and tear gas is a memory. Wooden boards have replaced smashed windows.

It took Anita Lollchand, 68, five days to muster the courage to leave her apartment in search of groceries after the street, where she has lived for 40 years, devolved into a lawless zone of break-ins, looting, burglary and arson. In her building, young masked men burst into the foyer, ripped out the intercom and hammered at the glass on a second door. The glass cracked but didn’t give, and she trembles at the thought of what might have happened had they gotten through.

“We’ve seen so many protests here,” she said, breaking into tears. “This wasn’t a protest. It was a revolt.”

Oct. 17 marked a dark day in France. Large, peaceful demonstrations across the country were overtaken by riots, attacks on government buildings and looting. While admitting failures of security and intelligence, the government blamed both far-left insurgents and opportunistic delinquents.

The French Chamber of Commerce and Industry released its grim accounting this week. About 2,500 businesses across France were affected, and 47 percent of them were severely damaged. Some 480 were in the Paris region.

A small, curving street that unfurls from Place de la République — the city’s favored site for left-wing gatherings — Rue Beaurepaire sustained heavy damage. On its three short blocks, there were smashed windows, three building fires, and break-ins and looting in at least eight stores and two apartment buildings.

BLVD. de MAGENTA

1/4 mile

10TH ARRONDISSEMENT

Canal Saint-Martin

Rue BEAUREPAIRE

Paris

Place de la République

France

Detail

area

Paris

Seine

2 miles

The New York Times

While some businesses have gone back to normal, serving cafés crèmes in the morning and Cambodian bowls to the lunch crowd, many locals say they are still trying to make sense of what happened on a street they had considered lively and friendly.

“This country is already falling apart,” Rudy Zylbersztejn, 32, said from behind his chrome counter inside Deni’s Bagels, which he opened with his brother six months ago. Thugs tried to break through their storefront window that day, but the reinforced glass only cracked.

“We’re destroying ourselves,” Mr. Zylbersztejn added.

A 19th-century street, Rue Beaurepaire was the site of barricades defended by young teenagers during the final bloody days of the Paris Commune, the short-lived revolutionary government that ruled Paris in the spring of 1871.

Because of its proximity to the Place de la République, Rue Beaurepaire’s modern-day residents and store owners are used to protests. But nothing like this.

The day began with shop owners opening a few hours before the march planned by students and union groups, protesting poor conditions in high schools and the rising cost of living.

But the crowd differed from the usual protesters, said Didier Mondragon, the franchise owner of a small Franprix grocery store at the start of Beaurepaire. They were younger, dressed in black and wearing masks, he said. Acting on instinct, he closed the store around 1:30 p.m., pulling down metal shutters over the storefront while he and his workers had lunch and waited inside in hopes of reopening later.

Just over an hour later, the exterior security camera revealed a strange scene — people dressed mostly in black appeared like a flash mob, and, forming a group, they jumped up and down in unison. Inside, the store echoed with noise as the group kicked and hit the shutters. Mr. Mondragon and his staff had just enough time to take refuge in the basement before the mayhem erupted.

Over the next three hours, people poured into the store. They smashed fridge doors, threw over shelves, cracked into cash registers and left the floor covered with discarded jars and packages. They stole up to 200,000 euros of merchandise, he estimated, along with about 45,000 euros in cash they took from the safe.

One of his customers, Sophia Costa, was in her second-floor apartment across the street watching with horror as people attacked the pharmacy next door to the grocery. They didn’t seem to be looting for themselves. Instead, they grabbed items from the shelves and tossed them into the road, like carnival workers.

She saw people throwing bottles and breaking a second-story window across from her, the site of a physiotherapy clinic, where some walls were stained with iodine that appeared to have been looted from the pharmacy and tossed into the clinic.

Worried that they might attack her windows too, Ms. Costa closed her shutters. Soon, she smelled smoke. Beneath her, a legal assistance office had been broken into and set on fire. The pharmacy across the street was also burning, along with a bar down the block.

At one point, four fire trucks roared onto the street.

Around 5 p.m., Ms. Costa heard people running up her building’s stairwell, shouting “get out” and “fire.” They banged on her door.

She found herself face to face with some of the same people she believed had set the fires, now inside warning residents of the danger. It was just one confusing thing about that day.

“There were a lot of contradictions,” said Ms. Costa, 22, a decorative painter who moved to France from Italy.

Two blocks down, Habib Saïdi stationed himself in front of the clothing store Agnès B., a French chain where he has worked for more than two decades. Groups of young men dressed in black approached to push the windows and test the door locks, he said. One carried an iron bar, another pliers. “They were equipped,” he said.

Unarmed, Mr. Saïdi repeated the same plea: “This is my store.” It worked; the store was spared. He, like many other people on Rue Beaurepaire, said he had alerted the police. But no officers arrived.

“We were completely left to fend for ourselves and abandoned by the police,” said Mr. Saïdi, who runs security for the company. The Paris police did not respond to a request for comment. At least two people were convicted of stealing from the Franprix.

There was not just rioting and looting. There was also organized robbery. When Ms. Lollchand, the longtime resident, ventured out with her son around 11 p.m., she saw men sawing into the metal shutters of the Boxing Shop up the street, and then hurrying packages into their waiting van. Ms. Costa, who also went outside later, encountered two girls who tried to sell her boxing gloves from the store.

The scene was enough to keep Ms. Lollchand inside for days.

The chaos continued the next day.

Emmanuelle Leonardi, a brand manager for the clothing designer Petite Mendigote, learned from a live news broadcast that the company’s storefront on Rue Beaurepaire had been smashed open and was being looted.

Dozens of black-clad thieves made off with thousands of euros’ worth of clothes and bags, she said. The company would have fared worse had it not been for a local resident, Sofía Serna Ángel, who confronted the gang in front of the shop’s broken window.

“I started stopping the people who were leaving with stuff, telling them, “That’s really cowardly, it’s not right — you’re ruining people’s lives,” said Ms. Ángel, who is in her thirties. Most of the thieves, she said, appeared as young as 12. Many, she said, were polite. The riots had not only damaged stores, she noted, they unjustly polluted the protests’ cause.

Other neighbors joined her to stand vigil before the broken window for hours, ensuring the looters stayed away.

“It shows that there is a collective conscience after all,” Ms. Leonardi said. “That’s why I still have hope.”

The next morning, many neighbors arrived to help clean, Ms. Leonardi said. Others started fund-raisers to help the store owners rebuild. Ms. Costa said she met many of her neighbors for the first time as they fled their burning building together. They have since met for drinks.

“There is a little light after the storm,” said Mr. Mondragon, the Franprix owner, who hopes to rebuild and reopen his store within a few months, after insurance kicks in.

Many on the street are bracing for more protests on Saturday and beyond. “What are they going to look like?” Mr. Mondragon said. “In a month, in a year, we will always have this apprehension, wondering what is going to happen.”

He added, “It was hell.”

item.title: Syria Weighs Joining Saudi Mutual Defense Pact as Yemen War Rages
item.description:
Syria is considering joining a regional defense alliance with Saudi Arabia, its foreign minister said on Saturday, raising the prospect that Damascus could become involved in the kingdom’s widening conflict with the Iran-backed Houthi militia in Yemen.

Asaad al-Shaibani, the Syrian foreign minister, told the Manama Dialogue security conference in Bahrain that “discussions are currently underway to evaluate Syria’s entry into the Mecca alliance,” referring to a mutual-defense pact signed in August by Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan.

Under the terms of the pact, known as the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, an armed attack on any of its three members would be considered an attack on all, mirroring NATO’s collective-defense principle. The countries agreed this month to prepare for the rapid deployment of military forces to Saudi Arabia as the Houthis have intensified their attacks on the kingdom.

Mr. al-Shaibani said that Syria regarded the defense of Gulf Arab countries as essential to its own security. “Syria will stand beside all of the Gulf countries,” he said, adding that they faced challenges from “militias that cross borders.”

It was unclear, however, whether that potential support would extend to sending Syrian troops to Yemen.

Since sweeping to power almost two years ago, President Ahmed al-Sharaa of Syria has sought to stay out of regional conflicts, as his government has struggled to rebuild the country after nearly 14 years of civil war. The Syrian authorities denied reports this month that Saudi Arabia had requested that Syrian troops be deployed, saying Damascus was focused on reconstruction.

But Syria’s growing ties with Saudi Arabia could complicate that position, analysts say. Saudi Arabia has become a major diplomatic and economic supporter of Syria since the country’s longtime dictator, Bashar al-Assad, was overthrown by rebels led by Mr. al-Sharaa. The Assad family, which ruled Syria with an iron fist for more than five decades, had been closely allied with Iran, Saudi Arabia’s regional rival.

This month, Mr. al-Sharaa met with Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Saudi Arabia’s de facto leader, in Riyadh, where they discussed investment and regional security, according to a statement from the Syrian president’s office.

Syria has raised the possibility of joining the defense pact as fighting in Yemen and attacks on Saudi Arabia have intensified after years of relative calm.

After the Houthis seized the Yemeni capital, Sanaa, in 2014, Saudi Arabia began a disastrous bombing campaign the following year in support of the country’s internationally recognized government. The fighting largely subsided after a United Nations-brokered truce in 2022, but it has escalated this year amid the broader U.S.-Israeli war with Iran.

The renewed fighting has killed at least 1,677 people and wounded more than 7,300 in Yemen since August, according to the World Health Organization. Nearly 300,000 Yemenis have been displaced, the United Nations has said, deepening a devastating humanitarian crisis in one of the world’s poorest countries.

In Saudi Arabia, Houthi missile and drone attacks on airports and vital infrastructure have killed at least 19 people and wounded hundreds more, according to the Saudi-led military coalition. The escalating attacks, which have severely disrupted air travel, have increasingly threatened the kingdom’s ambitions to become a global tourism and business hub.

As the attacks have intensified, Egypt — which is not part of the Mecca pact — this week authorized military aid to Saudi Arabia, another sign of the growing regional response to the conflict.

On Saturday, the Saudi-backed coalition said it intercepted three drones over the kingdom, including one near the capital, Riyadh. In Yemen, six people, including three children, were wounded in what the Houthi authorities said was a Saudi airstrike on a grocery store in Taiz Province.

Taiz, one of Yemen’s largest cities, has become a major battleground in recent weeks. The Houthis have cut road access to the strategically located city, leaving its residents with dwindling supplies of food, water and fuel.

Taiz is at a crossroads between Houthi-held territory in the north of the country and the government-controlled south and the Red Sea coast. Taking control would help the Houthis increase pressure on government forces and cement control of coastal areas on the Red Sea.

In another development, the Houthis have come under renewed scrutiny for arresting a number of U.N. personnel and aid workers two years ago. On Saturday, the United Nations said that Mohammad el Shami, a Yemeni employee of its human rights office who had been detained since June 2024, had died in custody.

Volker Türk, the U.N. human rights chief, called for an independent investigation into his death.

item.title: Poland Deploys Riot Police in Standoff Over Country’s Top Court
item.description:
Poland’s centrist government deployed riot police at the country’s Constitutional Tribunal late Friday, amid an escalating confrontation between the prime minister, the president and allies of the previous right-wing government.

The police intervention followed an effort Friday by a group of government-backed judges to take control of the tribunal, the nation’s top court, from its chief justice, who is aligned with the previous government of Law and Justice, a hard-right nationalist party.

Ever since its election in 2022, the centrist coalition government of Prime Minister Donald Tusk has been feuding with Law and Justice, which lost power in that vote. Among the most critical issues in the feud is the composition of the Constitutional Tribunal, which Law and Justice stacked with right-wing judges under the previous government.

Poland’s president, Karol Nawrocki, who was elected last year with support from Law and Justice and President Trump, interrupted a trip to Senegal to rush back to Warsaw. His plane turned around midair so that the president, a bitter foe of the current government, could join the fracas at the Constitutional Tribunal.

The situation at the court was murky on Saturday: Inside, Mr. Nawrocki was in a standoff with the pro-government judges, while protesters in support of Law and Justice had gathered outside, held back by the police.

Bogdan Swieczkowski, the chief justice who was suspended by the government-backed judges, was not in the building. He said he would meet with allied judges on Saturday to decide what to do, adding that if the tribunal remained surrounded by the police, “We might end up issuing rulings from other locations.”

Adding to the confusion and acrimony, while the pro-government judges took control of the tribunal’s website, Mr. Swieczkowski’s supporters still held the court’s social media account, which they used to accuse their rivals of “committing the crime of a coup d’etat.”

For supporters of Prime Minister Tusk’s government, the struggle for control of the tribunal is an essential part of an effort by a democratically elected administration to reverse Law and Justice’s capture of the courts and other nominally independent institutions during its eight years in power between 2015 and 2023. Their opponents see it as an authoritarian push.

The election last year of Mr. Nawrocki as president, a largely ceremonial post, turned what had been a slow-burn struggle into a full-blown crisis when he refused to invite five new Constitutional Tribunal judges appointed by Parliament to the presidential palace to take their oaths.

Mr. Tusk’s government argues that the constitutional court, which has repeatedly blocked legislation enacted by Parliament, is illegitimate because several of its judges were appointed improperly during Law and Justice’s time in power. European courts ruled that these appointments meant that the Polish court was no longer an “independent and impartial tribunal,” but Law and Justice argues that these outside courts have no jurisdiction.

Mr. Tusk, in a post on X, said: “Restoring the rule of law is our duty. After years of Law and Justice’s lawlessness, this is a difficult, sometimes painful process that requires decisive action. There is no other way.”

With elections for a new Parliament looming next year, Mr. Tusk has come under increasing pressure from supporters to break the deadlock over the court so that the government can deliver on its legislative agenda before its time in office runs out.

Judges backed by Mr. Tusk’s government used the tribunal’s website to announce on Saturday that the chief justice, Mr. Swieczkowski, had been suspended from his duties. The move followed years of legal wrangling.

Mr. Swieczkowski tried later to enter the building after supporters of Law and Justice, who have held demonstrations outside the tribunal for weeks, cut a fence with power tools.

Warsaw’s police department, in a statement, said that it had sent officers to the court “in response to information provided by a judge of the Constitutional Tribunal, which indicated the potential for threats to the life or health of the Tribunal’s judges and staff, as well as a risk of public disorder.”

Anna Korwin-Piotrowski, a judge with a long career in the judiciary and a recent appointment to the Constitutional Tribunal, issued an order late Friday that the chief justice and his deputy had both been suspended.

She did this in her capacity as the Constitutional Tribunal judge with the longest judicial tenure and announced the move on Saturday on the tribunal’s website, now controlled by her allies.

Anatol Magdziarz contributed reporting.

item.title: Train Disaster Is a Blow to Spain’s Leader, Already an Election Underdog
item.description:
One month before Spain’s national elections on Nov. 29, Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez held a long meeting in Madrid’s Atocha station with officials from the train traffic control center that his government has blamed for a devastating crash that killed at least 69 people.

As his motorcade pulled away, Felis Caballero, a pharmaceutical company employee, rolled her luggage in front of the station.

“I travel a lot, and the train for me was always very safe, but not lately,” she said, adding that two mass-casualty accidents this year had eroded her faith in the rail system, and in Mr. Sánchez.

A self-described moderate from a town in central Spain near the site of the accident, Ms. Caballero, 60, said she wasn’t sure whether she would vote for the mainstream conservative opposition or cast a blank ballot. But one thing was clear, she said: It wouldn’t be for Mr. Sánchez’s Socialist Party. Under him, she said, things were “going badly.”

Mr. Sánchez, one of the longest-serving leaders in Europe, has faced his fair share of disasters during his eight years in power. Natural disasters have included the coronavirus outbreak, deadly floods in Valencia, wildfires and the eruption of a volcano in the Canary Islands.

He has governed through infrastructure nightmares, including a blackout across the country and a January train crash that killed 46 and was apparently caused by faulty rail on the track between Madrid and Seville. And just this summer, about 80,000 migrants breached Morocco’s border with the Spanish exclave of Ceuta in North Africa, though all but a few thousand soon returned to Morocco.

Perhaps the most damaging disasters to his fortunes have been political ones, including a raft of corruption scandals in his inner circle. One case put one of his closest advisers, the former public works minister who oversaw the railways, in jail.

Mr. Sánchez, a survival artist and talented campaigner, called early elections this month and earlier this week seemed to be hitting his stride. He joked around on a late-night talk show, chatted with YouTube influencers, sat for interviews with friendly media outlets. Then Wednesday’s horrific accident occurred.

It knocked Mr. Sánchez off a nascent charm offensive, and instead raised doubts about the competence that is core to his left-wing government’s pitch, and could dash the enthusiasm of the left-wing supporters he desperately needs to go to the polls and tighten his already narrow path to re-election.

“If blame falls on the government, an electoral penalty for them is the expected outcome,” said Ignacio Urquizu, the director of the independent polling firm Metroscopia and a former Socialist Party member of Parliament.

Mr. Sánchez’s government has been swift and unusually transparent this week in sharing information that it says shows that the fault for the crash rests with what the current transportation minister, Óscar Puente, has called the “inexplicable” negligence of traffic control operators. The conversations of those operators from the Madrid station to conductors of the two trains in the crash were leaked on the day of the accident.

Whereas evidence of human error individualizes fault and can contain political damage, Mr. Urquizu said, systemic failures tend to hurt governments because they are held accountable.

“When an incident happens a second time,” he said, “it acts as an aggravating factor.”

Mr. Sánchez, loath to seem politically motivated in the midst of a tragedy, has spoken every day near the crash site, clad in the kind of utility vest worn by emergency responders, and expressing support for them and for victims’ families. His focus, he has repeatedly said, is getting to the bottom of what happened.

“It is unacceptable for a country like Spain, with a high-speed system as powerful as the one we have, to suffer two accidents of this nature and magnitude in a single year,” he said on Friday. “What we are going to do is not only investigate the causes of what took place but also provide solutions to further strengthen the high-speed rail network.”

Mr. Puente, the transportation minister, who usually relishes his role as the government’s attack dog, insisted during a news conference on Friday that “I don’t have the electoral campaign on my mind.” He instead gave a chapter and verse description of the missteps of the traffic controllers that he said had caused the accident.

The government’s right-wing opponents, on the other hand, are trying to make the accident a symptom of a systemic problem, for which they hold Mr. Sánchez accountable.

“Attempting, as they did, to hold an operator at Atocha station responsible for a systemic failure across all safety layers is unprecedented,” said Alberto Núñez Feijóo, the leader of the Popular Party, Spain’s main opposition conservative party, who is favored in polls to win the election. “Everything that could fail, failed. The safety systems, the control center and the backup system. Every single layer.”

He said the government sought to deflect blame by faulting individual controllers. “If they don’t resign, we will vote them out at the ballot box.”

Santiago Abascal, the leader of the far-right party Vox, went even further. He has called Mr. Puente the “minister of death,” and at a rally on Thursday described Mr. Puente and Mr. Sánchez as a “sinister couple.”

Even before the crash, Mr. Sánchez faced an uphill climb in his bid to lead his fourth consecutive government since 2018.

He has sought to gain back momentum by talking about Spain’s significant economic growth, its declining unemployment, its attraction of immigrants and tourists, and its global status under his leadership as a progressive voice against President Trump and Israel’s war in Gaza.

Earlier this month, after protests erupted over unaffordable housing, his minority government sought and failed to pass measures popular with his left-wing base. He used the defeat in Parliament as an opportunity to call for early elections, hoping to gain momentum and enthusiasm with liberals, and to frame the election as a contest between moneyed elites and regular Spaniards whom he championed.

After the train crash, housing is less prominent on the national radar, and the country has retrenched into its deep polarization. With few undecided voters, enthusiasm within the country’s left and right blocs remains decisive.

In the last election, in 2023, Mr. Sánchez pulled off what many considered a political miracle by motivating his traditional left-wing base and cobbling together a coalition of far-left parties supported in Parliament by secessionist movements, in part by scaring them all to his side with a vision of a coming far-right government.

This time, experts say, Vox is more familiar and the threat less effective, and he is struggling to mobilize the left. His aides, confident in the prime minister’s campaign-trail talents and robotic ability to stay on message, had painstakingly planned a campaign schedule for him to hit inflection points like a national strike next month. The idea was to crest on a wave of enthusiasm before Election Day.

Then a Seville-bound high-speed train plowed into the back of a train sitting on the tracks.

The problem for Mr. Sánchez, said Mr. Urquizu, is that crises like the train crash “open cracks through which voters abstain or switch sides.” Infrastructure has not been high on the list of priorities for voters, he said, but the second train accident in a year “breeds distrust toward the government.”

item.title: North Korean Hackers May Have Stolen Billions. It Wouldn’t Be Their First Heist.
item.description:
Poor, isolated and heavily sanctioned, North Korea is not a country you would expect to field an elite army of hackers capable of pulling off billion-dollar heists.

But for years, security officials had warned that the regime’s cyberattacks were becoming increasingly sophisticated, looting enormous sums to support North Korea’s military and nuclear weapons program.

Those fears peaked this week when Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, said that hackers had made off with some $6 billion in what could be the biggest crypto heist in history. Crypto research firms quickly attributed the attack to North Korea, saying it bore the hallmarks of the country’s previous hacks — although officials have not confirmed the North’s role.

Powered by a pipeline of top-class programming students, North Korea’s hacking units have penetrated banks and companies and capitalized on the rise of crypto. A U.N. panel in 2024 found the regime’s cyberattacks had generated about half its foreign currency income, amounting to billions in revenue. Experts agree that the regime is now one of the biggest and most capable cyber threats in the world.

As investigators dig into the Binance attack, here is a look at some of the most famous North Korean hacks.

In 2014, the tech and media giant Sony Pictures was preparing to release “The Interview,” a far-fetched comedy about the assassination of the North’s leader.

Then, American officials said, hackers associated with the Lazarus Group, a shadowy hacking syndicate backed by the North Korean government, breached the company’s computers.

The attacks caused the leaks of internal documents containing salary information that humiliated top company officials and stole terabytes of data.

North Korea has never formally taken responsibility for the attack. At the time, however, Kim Jong-un, the country’s dictator, called the film an “act of terrorism.”

In 2016, North Korean hackers tried to steal about $1 billion from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. Only a spelling error stopped them.

Using a payment messaging system known as SWIFT, the hackers were able to persuade the New York Fed to move money to accounts in the Philippines. The hackers were looting an account of the Bangladesh Central Bank when bankers grew suspicious about a withdrawal request that had misspelled “foundation” as “fandation.”

Still, the hackers made off with $81 million from the central bank of Bangladesh.

The attack was important because it showed how savvy North Korean hackers were becoming. In contrast to off-the-shelf tools that had been used in other attacks at the time, the malware the thieves devised for this heist was a custom code, configured for a specific bank. Written from scratch, it was unfamiliar to existing virus-protection programs.

As the cryptocurrency market boomed in the mid 2010s, North Korea began targeting firms in the industry, escalating to large-scale attacks on crypto exchanges by 2020, according to a North Korea-focused publication of the Stimson Center, a Washington-based think tank.

North Korean hackers were accused of stealing $571 million from crypto exchanges between January 2017 and September 2018 and $316 million from 2019 to November 2020.

With borders shut because of the coronavirus pandemic and traditional banks strengthening their firewalls against hackers, cryptocurrency theft was becoming an increasingly vital source of foreign currency for the regime.

In 2022, the United States publicly accused the Lazarus Group of stealing $620 million in cryptocurrency from the video game Axie Infinity.

That year, North Korea’s haul was a little under $1 billion, according to Chainalysis, a crypto analytics firm, which found 50 percent of the industry’s yearly losses were from North Korean hacks.

Given the history of spectacular market crashes, crypto is hardly a stable source of funding. But at a time when North Korea had locked itself down during the pandemic, hacking crypto exchanges allowed it to generate income in ways that were both Covid-safe and harder to trace in an industry subject to limited government oversight.

In February 2025, North Korean hackers pulled off what was then the biggest heist in the crypto industry’s history, stealing $1.5 billion in cryptocurrencies, according to the F.B.I.

To pull off the breach, the hackers exploited the cryptocurrency exchange ByBit’s reliance on a free software product.

The North Korean hackers had tricked the chief executive of Bybit, Ben Zhou, into authorizing a seemingly routine transaction that handed them control of the exchange’s system.

After looting Bybit, the North Korean hackers spread the stolen funds across a vast web of online crypto wallets, a money-laundering strategy that they had also employed after other heists.

This week, that record was broken in the Binance hack. Hackers stole $6.3 billion in an attack that used “laundering patterns we have not seen before,” Chainalysis wrote in a blog post on Friday.

Binance initially said that the hackers might have compromised an engineer’s laptop, leading to unauthorized withdrawals. But in an update on social media on Friday, the company said it had identified “additional points of breach.”

The specifics of the attack are still being established. TRM Labs, a crypto research firm, said it appeared to be the work of TraderTraitor, which the F.B.I. says is another name for the Lazarus Group.

But U.S. officials have not yet publicly attributed the hack to North Korea.

item.title: Clashes Erupt Again in France, After Festive Start to Day of Protest
item.description:
Hundreds of thousands of people poured into the streets of French cities again on Saturday for protests that began with the festivity of a Halloween parade but gave way to darker scenes of clashes between demonstrators and the police.

The violence fell well short of the arson and looting that engulfed Paris and other cities on Oct. 17, when a mass demonstration muted into widespread lawlessness. The crowds, estimated by the government at 320,000, were also smaller than on the previous two Saturdays of nationwide protest.

Still, the turnout — and the chaos — was significant enough to suggest that France remains in the grip of acute unrest, nearly two months into a protest movement that began with rebellious high school students.

In several cities, the police fired tear gas and sprayed water cannons to disperse some protesters after what had been peaceful rallies. In Paris, 200 to 300 rioters, masked and clad in black, skirmished with police officers into the evening, lobbing Molotov cocktails, fireworks and other projectiles.

It was a discordant end to a day that had begun on an upbeat, even joyful, note. Many people made the most of the fact that the demonstration coincided with Halloween. They showed up in eye-catching costumes, as Spider-Man, Zorro or the Pink Panther, dancing as often as they marched. One, dressed as Marie Antoinette, held a sign that said, “Let them eat cake.”

French officials had said they worried that the holiday would introduce a dangerous element, since demonstrators might conceal their faces. They marshaled 70,000 police officers, the same number as last week, and shifted routes to keep the protesters away from city centers.

France’s interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, condemned what he said were violent rioters, with links to the far left, who mixed in with the protesters. Many of them broke into clashes with the police as the marches ended and the authorities tried to disperse the crowds.

On Saturday evening, Mr. Nuñez said, the police in Paris were still confronting “groups that intend to head to the Bastille,” the site of an uprising in 1789 that is a milestone in the French Revolution. The Paris authorities had prevented the march from starting there.

“The intent is to create an insurrectionary climate — a quasi-revolutionary atmosphere — and to attack domestic security forces in order to gain access to stores, to carry out looting, to attack public buildings, and they are attacking law enforcement in an extremely violent manner,” Mr. Nuñez said.

In Paris, television images showed the police coming under attack by fireworks and Molotov cocktails. At least one officer was briefly engulfed in flames, an attack that Mr. Nuñez said qualified as attempted murder. Trash bins were set alight, as was a car. Similar chaotic scenes played out in Marseille, Rennes, Nantes, Toulouse, Montpellier, Angers and Tours.

Marine Le Pen, the far-right leader and presidential candidate, condemned the targeting of police officers, writing on social media that the “perpetrators of this attack must be found and sentenced with the utmost severity.”

Jean-Luc Mélenchon, a far-left leader who is also running for president, accused the government of undercounting the crowds. He claimed they were as large as previous demonstrations, despite the change in the route.

The police arrested 565 people, which Mr. Nuñez said prevented a worse outbreak of violence. The authorities also carried out 40,000 spot checks across the country to prevent people from taking weapons to protest areas.

But Mr. Nuñez was careful not to declare victory. The Interior Ministry warned that the violence could intensify long after darkness fell. On Saturday night, bands of people still roamed Paris and other cities. “We will remain vigilant throughout the evening and the night,” he said.

It was a stark contrast to earlier in the day, when people began massing for the marches. Brass bands played music, and the protesters’ costumes provided a celebratory atmosphere. Several people said they wanted to help reverse the narrative set on Oct. 17, when the marches mutated into violence, with gangs smashing shop windows and looting the contents.

“I’m really worried about how the riots have been instrumentalized by the far right,” said Helen Olive, 50, who was among a group of parents who had dressed as “super parents.” “We want to turn that narrative around.”

Arthur Fleury, a 20-year-old literature student, came as a prisoner riding a dinosaur and wearing a mask of Ms. Le Pen, the far-right leader. “Protests are about making demands but also having fun,” he said. “I was going for an absurd costume to capture the spirit of the movement.”

As the crowd marched along its route in eastern Paris, a bystander dropped candy from his balcony, drawing cheers. But there were already signs of trouble. Half a dozen masked protesters in black pushed trash bins, one of which was burning, into the middle of the crowd. They set a second bin on fire near where a police unit was stationed.

Other demonstrators used water to put out the fire, precipitating a small clash with the masked group. “That’s no way to protest,” said one of those who helped put out the fire.

Among the protesters were Morgane Voisin, 22, and Corentin Schnell, 19, both of whom wore white outfits identifying them as “street medics” able to deliver first aid. Ms. Voisin, a sales consultant, said she participating because her younger siblings had faced harsh conditions in high school.

Mr. Schnell, an engineering student, said he joined after his younger brother told him he was tear-gassed and almost struck by a stun grenade at a protest this month.

“The mere fact that people are being injured by the police makes me furious,” Mr. Schnell said. “So, I’ve come to demonstrate and to try to provide medical care — to limit the damage, regardless of which side it’s on.”

On Saturday, the two said they saw one person who had been injured in the head. Help arrived quickly. “Long live youth!” Ms. Voisin said.

Giulia Imbert contributed reporting.

item.title: ‘We Are Coming From Hell’: A Ukrainian City’s Evacuees Tell Survival Stories
item.description:
A rasping scream rang out as a teenager recognized her father. He was one of the hundreds of people who had escaped: years of Russian occupation, months of hunger under a deadly drone war, and then a truce backed by a first lady and the pope and an odyssey back to their loved ones.

A fleet of buses brought the evacuees from the embattled Ukrainian city of Oleshky out of the war zone on Saturday, the passengers waving and wiping tears as they swung into the parking lot and ended their journey back.

Draped in Ukrainian flags, the evacuees stepped down gingerly from the buses, weary after a 24-hour journey, which took them from the front line and through Russia and Belarus before returning to Ukraine. Many were gaunt from living months with little food, dark rings round their eyes from lack of sleep.

“We are coming from hell,” said Oleksandr Styopin, 75, lighting a cigarette. “It’s a kill zone there.”

Trapped close to the front line, with Russian soldiers living among them, the residents of Oleshky have been living under occupation for more than four years since Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022.

Their predicament worsened this year, when Ukraine drastically increased its drone attacks on Russian forces in the area, said Mr. Styopin, a retired electrical engineer.

The roads came under fire and supplies dried up as fewer and fewer drivers dared to risk the trip. Some residents tried to drive to the nearby town of Radensk to buy provisions, but many were killed on the road when drones struck their vehicles, he said.

Bodies of Russian soldiers were left lying in the road, he said, since no one would risk collecting them.

Mr. Styopin would push his bike to a local store once in a while and stock up on as much food as he could carry. Once he passed the burned body of a girl beside her own bicycle, he said. “That was from a mine, I think,” he said.

Some drones hovered close as if to look at him, and then let him be, he said.

But they hunted down the Russian soldiers relentlessly, he said.

“They pinned them down so hard, they could not step out of the building,” he said of the Russian soldiers. A group of soldiers had moved into an apartment in his building, he said.

Some of the evacuees described the hardships they endured with a lightness that verged on humor as they recalled destruction and loss.

“There was no electricity and no water. Then the house got bombed. Then the food ran out,” said Halyna Lohvynovska, 65.

“We got used to everything,” her husband, Ivan Lohvynosky, said with a smile. Their house was hit several times, he said. “When something fell on your head, you moved to another room. When the house was destroyed more, you moved house.”

There were some young families and even young children among those evacuated.

Vladyslav, 24, came out with his sister and mother. Thin and watchful, he declined to give his surname for security, he said.

The family had stayed in Oleshky because they had been scared that the Russian authorities would prevent him from leaving; he was of the age to be drafted into the military in Ukraine.

They survived by growing vegetables in their garden and raising a few animals, he said.

To some of their fellow evacuees, that was good fortune.

“The past two years were terrible. We had nothing to eat,” said Anatolii Honcharov, 53. His 61-year-old brother, Valerii, had not heard from him for three years because communications were so bad. Only families who lived close to the river could pick up a Ukrainian cellphone signal.

Things became so dangerous in recent months, Mr. Styopin said, that he did not dare leave his apartment. He sat listening to the radio, a cigarette permanently clamped between his teeth, he said.

His wife, who left at the onset of the full-scale invasion in 2022, joining their son in Queens, New York, called him many times urging him to leave.

“If I try to leave, I will step on a mine,” he told her.

“For the last two months I was living with a drone above my head,” he added. “It’s more than fear,” he said, “it’s an internal dread that’s always present inside you.”

But the plight of Oleshky drew international attention, helping to push for a rare localized truce in a war where each side has pressed for every advantage. Pope Leo XIV, just three days after surgery for lung cancer, spoke with President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia and called for a cease-fire to evacuate the city, and then the American first lady, Melania Trump, announced a local truce last Friday.

When the cease-fire began on Tuesday, Russian soldiers appeared to demine the roads and clear the streets of the dead.

“The Russians cleared up everything,” Mr. Styopin said. “There was a destroyed armored personnel carrier with bodies inside,” he added. “There was a body in pieces, half here and half there. The Russian took them all away.”

Many residents did not trust the news of a humanitarian convoy. Several said they had tried to leave in convoys early in the war only to retreat after the vehicles came under fire.

But Mr. Styopin packed his things. Then, on Friday morning as he was leaving his home, a blast knocked him back. During the Russians’ demining an explosion went off, and shrapnel ripped into his suitcase, he said.

He went back to find another case and then rushed through heavy rain for more than a mile to the bus.

“My heart was burning,” he said. “I thought I would crawl there in order to leave.”

Vladyslav said he and his family feared to trust that they would truly escape.

“These last four days, we didn’t believe we would make it out,” he said. “We thought it was just another provocation — they would declare a cease-fire and then blow us up along the way,” he explained. “We were terrified, but we went anyway, because there might not be another chance.”

Many of the evacuees and their families said they were surprised at the scale of the seriousness of the operation to get them to safety, and said it raised hopes for an end to the war.

Standing in the parking lot looking around, Vladyslav still looked uncertain.

“I can’t quite make sense of my mood yet,” he said. “Happiness. Being back under my own flag, hearing my own language.”
